experiments.title: Hold Your Breath: why must a dolphin come up for air?
experiments.context: In this experiment you time how long you can hold your breath, and then compare your time with animals who breathe air in the water.
experiments.question: How long can you hold your breath at rest, and after exercise? How long can air-breathing animals who live in water stay under?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many seconds can you hold your breath sitting still? Will it be longer or shorter after 30 star jumps? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You sit on the same chair, rest the same time, take one ordinary breath in and start the clock at the same moment. Only the thing you do before the hold changes. It is rest, or it is 30 star jumps. You do each twice, with a rest between.

materials.item: a phone or clock with a seconds hand, to time the holds
a chair
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Sit on a chair or the floor. Stop the moment you want to breathe. Never hold your breath in water. Do not breathe fast and deep before the hold. A child with asthma or a breathing problem should skip the star jumps.
experiments.record: Write the four times in the results table. Draw a bar for each. Then write one line comparing your best time with a dolphin.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with a hand on her chest while a parent holds a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still and count your breaths for one minute.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with her mouth closed and a parent holding a phone showing 32 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Breathe in normally, hold, and stop when you need to breathe.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps in a small clear space on a floor, with a parent counting.
setup.caption: 3. Do 30 star jumps. Sit down at once and hold your breath again.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down. Show your child the timer.
flow.say: We will time how long you can hold your breath. How many seconds do you think? Will it be longer or shorter after 30 star jumps? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how long you can hold your breath. Longer or shorter after jumping? Why?
flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason. Do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hold Your Breath. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Ask your child to sit still. Count out loud each time they breathe out for one full minute. Write the number.
flow.say: Sit still and breathe as you usually do. I will count each time you breathe out for one minute.
flow.kid: Sit still. Your grown-up counts your breaths for a minute.
flow.parent: A child at rest breathes out about 15 to 25 times a minute. Write the number to use in the maths section.
flow.context: In this step you count your normal breaths in one minute.

flow.do: Rest. Your child takes one normal breath in, holds, and says stop when they want to breathe. Time it in seconds. Rest for two minutes. Do it a second time.
flow.say: Take one normal breath in and hold it. Say stop when you want to breathe. I will time you. Stop at any time you like.
flow.kid: Breathe in once. Hold. Say stop when you must breathe. Rest. Try again.
flow.parent: Most children hold for about 20 to 45 seconds at rest. Praise every time, and never push the child to hold longer. Stop at once if your child feels dizzy.
flow.context: In this step you time two breath holds at rest.

flow.do: Ask your child to do 30 star jumps. Then they sit down and hold their breath, as before. Time it. Rest for three minutes. Do it again.
flow.say: Now do 30 star jumps. Sit down at once, take one breath in and hold. Say stop when you must breathe. I will time you.
flow.kid: Do 30 star jumps. Sit. Breathe in once. Hold. Say stop.
flow.parent: Expected: the holds after star jumps are shorter, often by 10 to 20 seconds. After exercise, your muscles have used more oxygen and made more carbon dioxide, which makes you want to breathe sooner.

check.q: After star jumps, why do most people have to breathe sooner?
options: Their muscles used up oxygen and made more carbon dioxide
Their lungs got smaller
The air got thinner
check.why: Moving muscles use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, and the body wants to breathe out the carbon dioxide and breathe in oxygen. If you chose another answer, think about what your muscles were doing.

flow.context: In this step you time two breath holds after exercise.

flow.do: Read your child these air-breathing animals. A Ganges river dolphin comes up every minute or two. An emperor penguin can stay under more than 20 minutes. A sperm whale can stay under more than an hour. A rohu never needs to come up, because she has gills. Ask for three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.say: Now compare. Your best time was how long? A river dolphin comes up every minute or two. A penguin can stay under for over 20 minutes. A rohu never has to come up. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Compare your time. Say what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: air-breathing animals who live in water must come to the surface. What I saw: my time was short, and shorter after exercise. Why: lungs hold air, not water, so any animal with lungs must come up to refill. Some animals hold their breath much longer than people, but they all come up. A fish takes oxygen from the water with gills, so she can stay under for ever.
flow.context: In this step you compare your result with animals who breathe air in water.

experiments.title: Lump or Powder: why do gills have so many folds?
experiments.context: In this experiment you dissolve sugar in three forms to see how the shape of a thing changes how fast water works on it. Then you link the result to the folds of a fish's gills.
experiments.question: Does sugar dissolve faster as one whole lump, as broken pieces or as a powder?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which form of sugar will disappear in the water first? Which will take longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each glass gets the same amount of warm water and the same amount of sugar, from the same kind of cube. No one stirs. Only the form of the sugar changes. The whole cube is the control.
results_table: Time until no grains are left (seconds)

materials.item: 3 clear glasses
warm tap water, about 150 millilitres in each glass, as warm as for washing your hands
3 sugar cubes of the same kind, or 3 equal lumps of kalkandu (rock sugar)
a clean cloth and the back of a spoon
a phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. It must not be hot.
experiments.record: Write the three times in the table. Draw a bar for each. Then draw a rough picture of a fish's gill, and a simple lump, to show what is different.

setup.art: Three glasses of warm water on a table, with a whole sugar cube, a cube broken into pieces and a pile of powder beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Set out three glasses. Prepare the three forms of sugar.

setup.art: A child tipping the three forms of sugar into the three glasses at the same moment, with a parent holding a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Add all three at the same moment. Do not stir.

setup.art: Three glasses in a row with the powder gone, the pieces nearly gone, and the whole cube still half there.
setup.caption: 3. Watch. Write down the time when each one is gone.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down. Show your child the three forms of sugar.
flow.say: Here is sugar in three forms. One cube. One cube broken in pieces. One cube crushed to powder. Which will disappear in the water first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three forms of sugar. Which disappears first? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lump or Powder test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 150 millilitres of warm water into each of three glasses. Leave one cube whole. Break the second cube into about 6 pieces. Wrap the third cube in a cloth and press it with the back of a spoon until it is powder.
flow.say: Same water, same sugar. Only the shape of the sugar is different. Whole. Broken. Powder.
flow.kid: Fill three glasses. Make a lump, pieces and powder.
flow.parent: Hand-warm water is best. If the cubes are not equal, use the two most alike. Do the pressing on a table, not a glass.
flow.context: In this step you prepare the three forms of sugar.

flow.do: Start the timer. Tip each form into its own glass at the same moment, without stirring. Watch the glasses. Say the time out loud when no grains are left in each glass.
flow.say: Ready? Tip them in. Don't stir. Watch carefully. Which one goes first? Tell me when each glass looks clear.
flow.kid: Tip all three in at once. Do not stir. Say when each one is gone.
flow.parent: Expected: the powder is gone in under a minute, the pieces in a few minutes, and the whole cube takes longest, often 4 to 8 minutes. Stop at 10 minutes and write 'not finished' if the cube is still there. Cold water is slower, so use warm water.
flow.context: In this step you start the timer and watch the sugar dissolve.

flow.do: Write the three times. Ask why the powder was fastest. Then say that a fish's gill is a stack of thin folds, so water can touch a huge area of thin skin.
flow.say: Which form dissolved first? What was different about the powder? Water can only act on sugar where they touch. A powder has far more places to touch.
flow.kid: Which form was fastest? Why? Water works where it touches.

ask.q: Why did the powder dissolve fastest?
good: There was more sugar touching the water.

flow.parent: The same idea explains gills. A fish's gill is made of thousands of thin folds, so a lot of thin skin touches the water at once and oxygen passes into the blood quickly. Your lungs work the same way, with millions of tiny air sacs. The total area of a human lung is estimated at roughly 50 to 70 square metres, about the size of a badminton court. This is an analogy, because sugar and oxygen are different things.

check.q: Why would a gill with many thin folds take in oxygen faster than a flat gill of the same size?
options: More of the gill touches the water
The folds make the water warmer
The folds make the fish heavier
check.why: Oxygen passes in where the gill touches water, so more folds mean more touching. If you chose another answer, think back to the sugar. The powder touched the water in most places and dissolved fastest.

flow.context: In this step you read the results and connect them to gills.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: the more places water can touch, the faster it works. What I saw: the powder dissolved before the pieces and the pieces before the whole cube. Why: the powder has far more surface touching the water.
flow.context: In this step you say what you found out.

activities.title: Bat, Crow, Cat: which two belong together?

materials.item: a phone or a book with pictures of a bat, a crow and a cat
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess which two belong together. Sort the three animals in three ways. Say which sort tells you most about their families.

activities.record: A table with three animals and three ways to sort them, and one line saying which sort shows who is related.
activities.context: In this activity you look at a bat, a crow and a cat. You find that different rules put different animals together.

setup.art: A phone showing pictures of a bat, a crow and a cat side by side on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the three animals.

setup.art: A table drawn on paper with three columns: bat, crow and cat, and rows named moves, cover and babies.
setup.caption: 2. Write what each animal does and is made of.

setup.art: Three sorting rings on paper, each with two animals together and one apart.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the animals three times, once for each row.

flow.do: Show the three animals. Ask your child which two belong together, and why. Write down the answer.
flow.say: Look at a bat, a crow and a cat. Which two do you think belong together? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at a bat, a crow and a cat. Which two belong together? Why?
flow.parent: Most children say the bat and the crow because both fly. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bat, Crow, Cat activity. You guess before you sort.

flow.do: Make a table with the three animals. Fill in three rows. Moves: the bat flies, the crow flies, the cat walks. Cover: the bat has fur, the crow has feathers, the cat has fur. Babies: the bat and the cat have live young who drink milk. The crow lays hard-shelled eggs. Sort the animals once for each row.
flow.say: Let's sort them three ways. By how they move, which two go together? By their cover? By how their babies start?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Sort three times. Which two go together each time?
flow.parent: Expected: moves puts the bat with the crow. Cover and babies each put the bat with the cat.

check.q: Sorted by how they move, the bat goes with the crow. Sorted by cover and babies, she goes with the cat. Which sorts show who is related?
options: Moves, because both fly
Cover and babies, because fur and milk are clues from the family
Neither sort shows anything
check.why: Flying is a way of moving that has started more than once. Fur and milk are clues that come from an ancestor shared with the cat. If you picked flying, remember that insects fly too, and they are not related to birds.

flow.context: In this step you sort the three animals in three ways.

flow.do: Ask your child to say which sort they trust to find a bat's relatives, and why.
flow.say: Which sort do you trust to find a bat's relatives? Why?
flow.kid: Which sort shows a bat's family? Why?
flow.context: In this step you pick the sort that shows family.

activities.title: Same Bones, Different Jobs: feel your own arm

materials.item: a phone to look up pictures of skeletons of a bat wing, a dolphin flipper and a bird wing
paper and three coloured pencils: red, blue and green

schedule.what: Feel the bones in your arm. Look at pictures of other animals' limbs. Colour matching bones the same colour.

activities.record: A drawing of your arm bones and a drawing of a bat wing, with matching bones in matching colours.
activities.context: In this activity you feel the bones in your own arm and compare them with the bones in a bat's wing, a dolphin's flipper and a bird's wing.

setup.art: A child holding her upper arm with one hand and feeling the single long bone.
setup.caption: 1. Feel your upper arm. It holds one long bone.

setup.art: A child twisting her forearm and feeling two bones side by side below the elbow.
setup.caption: 2. Turn your forearm. Feel the two bones.

setup.art: A drawing of a human arm and a bat wing on paper with the bones coloured red, blue and green in matching order.
setup.caption: 3. Colour matching bones the same colour.

flow.do: Ask your child to hold their upper arm between the shoulder and elbow and squeeze. Ask how many long bones they can feel. Then ask them to turn the forearm over and feel between the elbow and the wrist.
flow.say: Hold your upper arm. Feel one long bone in the middle. Now hold your forearm and turn your hand over. How many bones can you feel?
flow.kid: Feel your upper arm. One bone. Turn your forearm. Feel two.
flow.parent: The upper arm has one bone, the humerus. The forearm has two, the radius and the ulna, and they cross when you turn your hand over.
flow.context: In this step you find the bones in your own arm.

flow.do: Search the phone for pictures of the skeleton of a bat's wing, a dolphin's flipper and a bird's wing. Look for one bone, then two bones, then a hand.
flow.say: Let's look at a bat's wing, a dolphin's flipper and a bird's wing. Can you find one bone, then two bones, and then something like a hand?
flow.kid: Look at the pictures. Find one bone, two bones and the hand.
flow.parent: Search for 'bat wing skeleton', 'dolphin flipper skeleton' and 'bird wing skeleton'. The bat has long finger bones. The dolphin has finger bones inside the paddle. The bird has fused fingers.
flow.context: In this step you look at the limbs of other animals.

flow.do: Draw your arm bones and a bat's wing bones. Colour the upper bone red, the two forearm bones blue and the hand bones green in both drawings.
flow.say: Draw your arm and a bat's wing. Colour the same bones the same colour. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Draw your arm and a bat's wing. Colour matching bones the same.

check.q: A human arm and a bat's wing have the same bones in the same order. What is the best explanation?
options: They inherited the plan from a shared ancestor
Both are for flying
A bat wing is a copy of a human arm
check.why: The same plan with different shapes is what you expect if both animals inherited the plan from one ancestor. A person's arm does not fly, so the job cannot explain the bones.

flow.context: In this step you draw and colour matching bones.

activities.title: No Backbone: one question for each group

materials.item: the 8 cards for animals with no backbone, which are cards 17 to 24 of the Group Detective printable
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Sort 8 animals with no backbone into piles by asking one question at a time.

activities.record: Six piles of animals, with the question written over each pile.
activities.context: In this activity you sort eight animals with no backbone into their big groups by asking one question at a time.

setup.art: Eight animal cards laid out in a row on a table: an ant, a spider, a crab, a snail, an octopus, an earthworm, a jellyfish and a starfish.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 8 cards face up.

setup.art: A child pulling the ant, the spider and the crab out of the row into a pile under the question: Does she have jointed legs?
setup.caption: 2. Ask the first question. Pull out every animal who fits.

setup.art: Four piles on a table, each with a question written on a sheet above it.
setup.caption: 3. Keep asking one question at a time until every card is in a pile.

flow.do: Lay the 8 cards face up. Ask your child to look at the facts. Ask the first question: does she have jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton? Put the yes cards in one pile.
flow.say: First question. Does she have jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton? Which animals say yes? Put them in one pile.
flow.kid: Ask: jointed legs and hard outer skeleton? Make a pile of the yes cards.
flow.parent: Expected: the ant, the spider and the crab are arthropods.
flow.context: In this step you ask the first sorting question.

flow.do: Ask the next questions for the remaining five cards. Does she have a soft body with a muscular foot? Does she have a soft body in rings with no legs? Does she have stinging tentacles? Does she have spiny skin and tiny tube feet? Make a pile for each yes.
flow.say: Next question. Soft body with a muscular foot? Put the yes cards in a pile. Then ask the rest, one at a time.
flow.kid: Ask each question. Make a new pile for every yes.
flow.parent: Expected: the snail and the octopus are molluscs. The earthworm is an annelid. The jellyfish is a cnidarian. The starfish is an echinoderm.

check.q: An octopus has no shell. Why is she still a mollusc?
options: She has a soft body and a muscular foot turned into arms, like a snail
She lives in the sea
She has eight arms
check.why: A mollusc is decided by her soft body and her muscular foot, not by the shell. An octopus has the same body plan as a snail, with the foot turned into arms. Many molluscs have no shell.

flow.context: In this step you ask the other four questions.

flow.do: Turn the cards over to check. Count how many piles you made. Ask why 'no backbone' is not one family.
flow.say: Turn the cards over. Did you get the same groups? How many separate groups did you find? Are they all one family?
flow.kid: Check the backs. How many groups? Are they one family?
flow.parent: Six kinds of animal with no backbone were sorted into 5 piles here. Sponges are the sixth group. They are as different from each other as a fish is from a snail.
flow.context: In this step you check the piles.

activities.title: One Animal, Two Shapes: tadpole and caterpillar

materials.item: 8 small pieces of paper
a pencil or coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw the stages of a frog and a butterfly. Put them in order. Decide which group each stage belongs to.

activities.record: Two rows of four small pictures, each in order of a life, with the group written under each row.
activities.context: In this activity you draw the stages of a frog and a butterfly and see why sorting an animal at one stage can mislead.

setup.art: Eight small cards on a table, four showing a frog's stages and four showing a butterfly's stages.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the four stages of a frog and of a butterfly.

setup.art: A child laying the frog cards in a row and holding the tadpole card up.
setup.caption: 2. Put each life in order.

setup.art: A child asking which group a tadpole would be put in if it were met alone.
setup.caption: 3. Ask which group each stage would go in if you met only that stage.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a frog's four stages on four cards. They are egg, tadpole, young frog and adult frog. Then draw a butterfly's four stages. They are egg, caterpillar, pupa and butterfly.
flow.say: Draw the four stages of a frog on four cards. Then the four stages of a butterfly.
flow.kid: Draw a frog's four stages. Draw a butterfly's four stages.
flow.parent: A pupa is the stage when the caterpillar's body is rebuilt inside a case. If your child does not know the stages, search for 'frog life cycle' and 'butterfly life cycle' on a phone.
flow.context: In this step you draw the stages of two lives.

flow.do: Hold up the tadpole card by itself. Ask which group your child would pick if they met only a tadpole. Ask which fact would show they were wrong.
flow.say: If you met only a tadpole, which group would you pick? Which fact would show you were wrong?
flow.kid: Look at the tadpole card. Which group would you pick? What shows you are wrong?

ask.q: What changes when the tadpole becomes a frog?
good: Her gills go and her lungs grow.

flow.parent: A tadpole has gills, a tail and lives in water, so she looks like a fish. The clues that she is an amphibian are her jelly eggs and what she will become. A caterpillar is an invertebrate, and so is the butterfly.

check.q: A tadpole lives in water and has gills and a tail. Why is she not a fish?
options: She will change into a frog with lungs and legs
She has no fins
She is too small
check.why: To sort an animal you look at her whole life, not one stage. A tadpole turns into a frog, so she is an amphibian. A fish keeps her gills for life.

flow.context: In this step you test what happens if you sort an animal at one stage.

activities.title: Draw the Backbone Family Tree

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
coloured pencils
8 small pieces of paper for the animal names

schedule.what: Draw a tree and put eight animals on the branches by asking four questions.

activities.record: A tree drawn on paper with four labelled branches and eight animals.
activities.context: In this activity you draw a family tree of eight animals with a backbone and put each animal on the branch where her group splits off.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a trunk drawn at the bottom and a label that says backbone.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a trunk. Write backbone on it.

setup.art: The tree with three branches splitting off one by one, labelled four limbs, sealed egg, and hair and milk.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the branches and write a new clue on each.

setup.art: The tree with small cards for a rohu, a shark, a frog, a gecko, a crocodile, a crow, a cat and a child placed on the branches.
setup.caption: 3. Put each animal on the last branch that fits her.

flow.do: Draw a tree trunk at the bottom of the paper and write Backbone on it. Draw a branch for each clue going up: four limbs, sealed egg, hair and milk. Write the clue on each branch.
flow.say: This tree has a trunk for the backbone. Each new branch adds one clue. Four limbs. Then a sealed egg. Then hair and milk.
flow.kid: Draw a trunk. Add three branches. Write a clue on each.
flow.parent: The branches get a clue each, as in the floor game rooms. The tree is a way of showing who is more closely related.
flow.context: In this step you draw the tree and write the clues.

flow.do: Write these eight animals on small pieces of paper: rohu, shark, frog, gecko, crocodile, crow, cat and you. Ask your child to put each on the last branch that fits. The rohu and the shark stay on the trunk.
flow.say: Put each animal on the last branch that fits her. The rohu and the shark have a backbone but no four limbs, so they stay low.
flow.kid: Put the eight animals on the branches. The fish stay low.
flow.parent: Expected: the frog on four limbs, the gecko, crocodile and crow on sealed egg, the cat and you on hair and milk.

check.q: Where does a crow go on the tree?
options: On the sealed egg branch, with the gecko and the cat
On the hair and milk branch
On the trunk with the rohu
check.why: A crow has a backbone, four limbs (the wings count) and an egg with a waterproof shell, so she goes on the sealed egg branch. She has feathers and no milk, so she does not go on the hair and milk branch.

flow.context: In this step you put the eight animals on the tree.

flow.do: Tell your child that crocodiles are closer relatives of crows than of geckos. Ask where that branch would be drawn. Ask why the tree is a better way than five boxes.
flow.say: Here is a surprise. A crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a gecko. How could we draw that on the tree?
flow.kid: A crocodile is closer to a crow than to a gecko. How do we draw that?
flow.parent: A good answer draws crocodile and crow on one short branch, and gecko on another. Five boxes cannot show this, but a tree can.
flow.context: In this step you add a surprise to the tree.

projects.title: A Wall Chart of the Backbone Family Tree

materials.item: a big sheet of chart paper or four sheets of paper taped together
coloured pencils or crayons
scissors and tape
pictures of 12 animals from old magazines or drawn by hand

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts out the pictures if the scissors are sharp.

schedule.what: Choose 12 animals with a backbone, including 3 you can see near home. Draw or cut out a picture of each and write her clues.
Draw the tree on the chart paper. Stick the animals on the branches. Add a hard case card and colour the rooms.

projects.record: The chart itself, with 12 animals, four labelled branches and two hard cases.
projects.context: In this project you make a wall chart of the backbone family tree with 12 animals, over two days.

setup.art: A table with 12 small animal pictures laid out and a list of clues beside each one.
setup.caption: 1. Choose 12 animals with a backbone and write her clues.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a tree drawn on it, with four labelled branches.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the tree with its four branches.

setup.art: The finished chart on a wall with the animals stuck on the branches and two animals in a special box labelled hard cases.
setup.caption: 3. Stick the animals on and add the hard cases.

flow.do: Choose 12 animals with a backbone. Include at least one fish, one frog, one reptile, one bird and one mammal, and three that you can see near home. Draw or cut out a picture of each. Write two clues under each picture.
flow.say: Let's make a chart of animals with a backbone. Choose 12. Include a fish, a frog, a reptile, a bird and a mammal. Write two clues under each.
flow.kid: Choose 12 animals. Draw each. Write two clues.
flow.parent: Include a hard case such as a bat, a dolphin or a penguin. The three animals near home might be a crow, a house lizard and a cat or a dog.
flow.context: In this step you choose and draw the 12 animals.

flow.do: Draw a tree on the chart paper with the four branches: backbone, four limbs, sealed egg, and hair and milk. Stick each animal on the last branch that fits her. Put two hard cases in a box beside the tree, with a note saying why they are hard.
flow.say: Now draw the tree and stick the animals on. Which animals will go where? Which two are hard cases? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the tree. Stick the animals on. Add two hard cases.
flow.parent: Hang the chart where the family can see it. Ask the child to explain one animal to a visitor.
flow.context: In this step you build the tree.

challenges.title: Write a Rule That Never Breaks
challenges.context: In this challenge you write one sorting rule for an animal group that no animal breaks, and test it against all 24 animal cards.
challenges.problem: Choose one group, such as birds or reptiles. Write one rule that puts every animal of that group in, and keeps every other animal out. Test it on the 24 animal cards.
constraints: The rule must be a question that anyone can check from the card.
The rule can use up to two clues together.
Test the rule on all 24 cards and count the animals it lets in or leaves out.
You may change the rule up to three times.
materials: the 24 animal cards from Group Detective
general: For birds: Animals with feathers are birds.
For mammals: Animals with hair or fur that feed milk are mammals.
For fish: Animals that breathe with gills all their lives are fish.
creative: For reptiles: Animals with dry scales and lungs. The fish have wet scales, and the amphibians have moist skin.
For amphibians: Animals with moist skin and lungs and skin together that lay jelly eggs in water or damp soil.
A rule that uses 'or' to cover both kinds, such as hair or feathers, to make a group of warm animals. Is that a real family?
challenges.your_turn: Pick a group and write your best rule. Test it. How many animals break it? Which clue did you use, and where did that clue come from?

setup.art: Twenty-four animal cards laid out in rows and a sheet of paper with a rule written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the cards. Write your rule.

setup.art: Two piles of cards, passes and does not pass, with a count written on a sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Test the rule and count the animals it lets in and leaves out.

flow.do: Pick one group. Write a rule. Lay out all 24 cards.
flow.say: Choose one group and write a rule for it. Then we will test your rule on all 24 animals.
flow.kid: Choose a group. Write a rule. Lay out the cards.
flow.context: In this step you pick a group and write your rule.

flow.do: Test the rule on all 24 cards. Count the animals it lets in and leaves out. Change the rule and test again.
flow.say: Does any animal break your rule? How many? Change the rule and try again.
flow.kid: Test the rule. Count the breakers. Fix the rule.
flow.context: In this step you test and mend your rule.

flow.do: Ask your child which clue they used and where that clue came from. Ask whether the rule might break on an animal not in the pile.
flow.say: Which clue did you use? Does it come from her body or from where she lives? Could an animal outside the pile break it?
flow.kid: Which clue did you use? Could another animal break it?
flow.context: In this step you think about how good your rule is.

challenges.title: The Alien Zoo: sort animals from another planet
challenges.context: In this challenge you invent ten animals from another planet and write sorting rules that work for them.
challenges.problem: Invent ten animals from another planet. Give each one four facts. Then sort them into groups with rules that no alien breaks.
constraints: Each alien has four facts, such as how she moves, what covers her, how she breathes and how her young start.
Write at least three groups and one rule for each.
At least one alien must be a hard case that nearly breaks a rule.
Swap your list with someone else and ask them to find a rule that breaks.
general: Sort by how the aliens move: crawl, swim or float.
Sort by what covers the body: fur, scales or shell.
Sort by how they get food: from the ground, from other aliens or from light.
creative: Sort by a clue you could only see with a microscope.
Sort by who could be related to whom, using a made-up family tree.
Make two different sorts for the same ten aliens and say which is better for a farmer, and which for a scientist.
challenges.your_turn: Which of your rules is the strongest? Which alien nearly broke it? How would you know whether two of your aliens were related?

quiz.p: How many kinds of animals have a backbone, compared with those that have none?
opts: Only about 1 in 20 kinds have a backbone
quiz.why: About 19 of every 20 named kinds of animals have no backbone. The animals with a backbone are the small half.

quiz.p: Which clue best shows that a bat is a mammal?
opts: She has fur and feeds her baby milk
quiz.why: Fur and milk are the clues for a mammal. Flying and hanging upside down are things she does, and a bird or an insect can do them too.

quiz.p: A penguin cannot fly. Why is he still a bird?
opts: He has feathers and lays hard-shelled eggs
quiz.why: Feathers and hard-shelled eggs decide a bird. A penguin swims instead of flying.

quiz.p: A rule leaves out an animal that belongs and lets in an animal that does not. What does this show?
opts: The rule is weak and needs a better clue
quiz.why: A rule that fails in both ways is weak. Scientists mend it by trying a body clue or two clues together.

quiz.p: Which animal is a hard case for the rule 'reptiles lay eggs'?
opts: A Russell's viper, who gives birth to live young
A house gecko, who lays eggs
quiz.why: A Russell's viper is a reptile with live young, so she breaks the rule. A gecko and a crocodile follow it.

quiz.p: A Ganges river dolphin must come up for air every minute or two. Why?
opts: She has lungs and no gills
quiz.why: A dolphin breathes air with lungs, so she must come to the surface. A fish has gills and can stay under.

quiz.p: Why do a bat's wing and a human arm have the same bones in the same order?
opts: Both came from an ancestor with that plan
quiz.why: The same plan used for different jobs is what you expect when both inherited the plan from one ancestor.

quiz.p: A tadpole should be sorted with the fish because she has gills.
quiz.why: False. A tadpole turns into a frog, and a fish keeps her gills for life. You must look at the whole life of an animal.

quiz.p: Which question separates a snail from an ant?
opts: Does she have jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton?
quiz.why: An ant is an arthropod with jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton. A snail is a mollusc with a soft body and one muscular foot.

opts: It only says what the animals lack, and they belong to many separate groups
All of them are the same shape
There are very few of them
quiz.why: The word names a missing backbone. Insects, snails and starfish are as different from each other as a fish is from a snail.

quiz.p: What is surprising about a lungfish?
opts: She is a closer relative of a cow than of a rohu
She is a kind of frog
quiz.why: A lungfish is a fish with lungs and fins that have bones. Her genes put her closer to land animals than to most fish.

quiz.p: A scientist finds an animal that lays eggs and also has fur and feeds milk. What should scientists do about the rule 'mammals give birth to live young'?
opts: Mend the rule so that milk decides a mammal
Say the animal is not a mammal
quiz.why: When evidence breaks a rule, scientists mend the rule. This is what happened with the platypus, so a mammal is defined by feeding milk.

items.p: What do all animals with a backbone have in common?
opts: A row of bones or hard cartilage down the middle of the back
items.why: A backbone is a row of small bones or hard cartilage. A shark, a snake and a bird have no legs or do not have four, and many have cold blood, so those are not the shared clue.

items.p: Most kinds of animals have a backbone.
items.why: False. About 19 of every 20 named kinds of animal have no backbone. Insects alone are more than a million kinds.

items.p: Animals with a backbone are called ____.
items.why: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. Animals with no backbone are called invertebrates.

items.p: Sort each animal by whether she has a backbone.
items.a: as given
items.why: A rohu, a crow, a cow and a gecko have a backbone. A snail, an ant, a jellyfish and a starfish have none.

items.p: Match each animal group to a clue that helps decide it.
pairs: Breathes with gills all her life
Thin moist skin and jelly eggs
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each group is decided by a few clues together. These are the main clue for each group.

items.p: A dolphin lives in water and has flippers. Why is she a mammal?
opts: She breathes air with lungs and feeds her baby milk
items.why: Breathing air with lungs and feeding milk are the clues that decide the group. Size and a tail do not.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Bat, crow, cat, cow.
items.a: Crow, because she has feathers and lays eggs. The other three are mammals with fur who feed milk.
items.why: A bat has fur and feeds milk, so she goes with the cat and the cow, even though she flies like a crow.

items.p: A rule says: animals that fly are birds. Which animal breaks this rule?
opts: A bat, who flies but is a mammal
A crow, who flies and is a bird
A cow, who does not fly
items.why: A bat flies, so the rule lets her in, but she is a mammal. A crow follows the rule and a cow does not enter it.

items.p: A platypus lays eggs, so she cannot be a mammal.
items.why: False. A platypus has fur and feeds her young milk, and those are the clues that decide a mammal. Laying eggs does not rule her out.

items.p: Zainab says: 'A penguin cannot fly, so a penguin is not a bird.' What would you say to her? Use a clue.
items.a: A strong answer says that the penguin has feathers and lays a hard-shelled egg. Those are the clues for a bird. Flying is not needed.
items.why: A strong answer names a clue that decides a bird, such as feathers or a hard-shelled egg, and says that flying is not the deciding clue.

items.p: A frog's young, who breathes with gills and has a tail, is called a ____.
items.why: A tadpole is a young frog. She changes shape into a frog with lungs and legs.

items.p: An ant has six jointed legs and a hard skeleton outside her body. Which group is she in?
items.why: Jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton are the clues for an arthropod. A mollusc has a soft body, and an annelid has a body in rings.

items.p: Draw your arm and a bat's wing side by side. Colour the bones that match in the same colour.
items.a: A drawing of an arm and a wing, each with one upper bone, two lower bones and finger bones, matching bones in matching colours.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one bone in the top part and two in the lower part of each, and the same colours for matching bones. It shows the same plan in a different shape.

items.p: Put these groups in order, from the biggest group to the smallest group that holds a house crow.
items.why: Each group sits inside the one before. A house crow is a bird, a bird has a backbone, and an animal with a backbone is an animal.

items.p: A snake has no legs. Which clue shows that she is a reptile?
items.why: Dry scales and lungs are the clues for a reptile. Having no legs and living on land are shared by many animals, such as worms and some lizards.

items.p: Why is 'where an animal lives' a weak clue for sorting animals? Give one example.
items.a: Animals who live in the same place can belong to different groups. For example, a dolphin, a shark and a sea turtle all live in the sea, but they are a mammal, a fish and a reptile.
items.why: A strong answer says that unrelated animals can live in one place, and gives an example such as a dolphin and a shark.

items.p: A shark and a dolphin both have a pointed, smooth body. What is the best explanation?
opts: Both swim fast, and that shape cuts through water well, so unrelated animals can end up with it
A dolphin is a kind of shark
A shark came from a dolphin
items.why: This is called convergent evolution. The two are on different branches of the tree of life, but the same problem gave them a similar shape.

items.p: Animals who look alike are always close relatives.
items.why: False. A shark, a dolphin and a penguin look alike but are a fish, a mammal and a bird. Clues from the body, such as milk or the bones, show who is related.

items.p: A bat's wing and a human arm have one upper bone, two lower bones and finger bones. What does this suggest?
opts: They inherited the plan from a shared ancestor
They are used for the same job
A bat is a kind of person
items.why: Different jobs but the same bones in the same order are what you expect if both inherited the plan from one ancestor.

items.p: A mammal is an animal who feeds her babies ____.
items.why: Feeding milk from her own body is the clue that decides a mammal, even for the egg-laying platypus.

items.p: Match each hard case to the group she belongs to.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each is a hard case. The climbing perch breathes air but has gills. The caecilian looks like a worm but has moist skin. The sea turtle breathes air. The ostrich cannot fly. The platypus lays eggs and feeds milk.

items.p: Sort each animal by how her babies start life.
items.a: as given
items.why: Cats, dolphins, bats and Russell's vipers are born live. Crows, geckos, platypuses and rohu hatch from eggs. Live birth appears in both mammals and reptiles, so it does not decide the group.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Octopus, snail, mussel, crab.
items.a: Crab, because she is an arthropod with jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton. The other three are molluscs with a soft body and a muscular foot.
items.why: An octopus, a snail and a mussel are molluscs. A crab has jointed legs, so she is an arthropod.

items.p: Which question best separates an insect from a spider?
opts: How many legs does she have?
items.why: An insect has six legs and a spider has eight. Both have no backbone, and both can live on land.

items.p: A friend says: 'A tadpole is a fish because she has gills, a tail and lives in water.' How could you show your friend that she is wrong?
items.a: Watch her over some weeks. She grows legs, her gills shrink and she grows lungs. She becomes a frog. A fish keeps her gills for her whole life.
items.why: A strong answer says that you must look at the whole life, and that a tadpole turns into a frog with lungs.

items.p: Mrs Kala's class is debating whether a whale shark and a dolphin should be in the same group, since both live in the sea and are huge.

views.who: Divya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Same group. They both live in the sea, they both swim and they are both huge. A group helps us find animals in the same place.

views.who: Ismail, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Different groups. The shark has gills and fins and the dolphin has lungs and milk. A group should show who is related.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you check?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example, it says that a group by habitat is useful for a fisher, and a group by body clues shows relatives.
items.why: Both views are useful for different jobs. A scientist who wants to know who is related uses body clues such as gills, lungs and milk.

items.p: Birds descend from small feathered dinosaurs. Which living animals are the closest relatives of birds?
items.why: The closest living relatives of birds are crocodiles. Lizards and snakes are on another branch.

items.p: The fossil Tiktaalik had fins with ____ bones and a neck, and lived about 375 million years ago.
items.why: Tiktaalik's fins held wrist bones, and she shows an animal in between a fish and a land animal.

items.p: Draw a family tree with a rohu, a frog, a crow and a cat. Show where each branch splits off.
items.a: A tree with a trunk for the backbone, with the rohu on the lowest branch, then the frog, then the crow and the cat on a branch of sealed eggs, with the cat on a final branch for hair and milk.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the rohu splitting off first, then the frog, and then the crow and the cat sharing a branch before splitting. It shows who is more closely related.

items.p: A lungfish is more closely related to a cow than to a rohu.
items.why: True. Genes show that lungfish are the closest living relatives of animals who walk on land, and a rohu is on a different branch of fish.

items.p: Why do scientists use two or three clues together to sort an animal?
opts: One clue can mislead, because animals who are not related can share it
Three is the rule in science
One clue is too hard to find
items.why: A clue such as flying or living in water is shared by animals on different branches. Two or three clues from the body are much harder to share by accident.

items.p: Why do animals with no backbone not make one family? Explain in one or two sentences.
items.a: Invertebrate only says what the animals lack. They belong to many separate groups, such as insects, snails and starfish, which are as different from each other as a fish is from a snail.
items.why: A strong answer says that the word names a missing feature and that the animals belong to many separate groups.

items.p: Design a better rule than 'animals that live in water are fish'. Say which clue you use and name one animal that broke the old rule.
items.a: Animals that breathe with gills all their lives are fish. A dolphin broke the old rule because she lives in water but breathes air.
items.why: A strong answer uses a body clue such as gills, and names an animal that lives in water but is not a fish, such as a dolphin or a sea turtle.

items.p: Whales and dolphins have four-legged ancestors. Which evidence supports this?
opts: Fossils of early whales from India and Pakistan had legs
items.why: Fossils such as Himalayacetus from India and Pakistan's early whales show animals with legs. DNA also shows that hippos are the closest living relatives.

items.p: A family-tree biologist and a bird watcher disagree about whether birds count as reptiles.

views.says: Birds descend from dinosaurs, which are reptiles, so birds are a branch inside the reptiles.
On a walk I need birds as a group of their own, because feathers and flight tell me how to find and identify them.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? When is each most useful?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and says that the biologist's view is useful for who is related, and the bird watcher's view for finding animals in the field.
items.why: The two views answer different questions. A family tree answers who is related, and a field guide answers how to find and name an animal.

items.p: If a rule has one exception, the whole group must be wrong.
items.why: False. A hard case shows that the rule is weak, not that the group is wrong. Scientists mend the rule with a better clue.

items.p: Which pair are the closest relatives?
items.why: Birds and crocodiles share a more recent ancestor than crocodiles and lizards do.

items.p: A rule can fail in two ways. It can leave out an animal that belongs, or it can ____ an animal that does not.
items.why: A rule that lets in an animal who does not belong has failed, as well as one that leaves out an animal who does.

items.p: Sort each animal into the smallest room of the family tree that fits her.
items.a: as given
items.why: A rohu has only the backbone. A frog has four limbs but no sealed egg. A gecko and a crow have sealed eggs and no milk. A dolphin and a bat have hair and milk.

items.p: An octopus has no backbone, and she can open a jar. What does this say about the idea that animals with a backbone are the cleverest?
items.a: It shows the idea is not right. Cleverness is found in animals without a backbone too. A backbone is not what makes a mind.
items.why: A strong answer says that an animal with no backbone can solve problems, so the backbone does not decide how clever an animal is.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Shark, rohu, dolphin, seahorse.
items.a: Dolphin, because she is a mammal who breathes air and feeds milk. The other three are fish with gills.
items.why: A shark, a rohu and a seahorse breathe with gills all their lives. A dolphin breathes air with lungs.

items.p: Match each hard case to the rule she breaks.
pairs: Animals that are born live are mammals
Animals that live in water are fish
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The penguin is a bird who cannot fly. The platypus is a mammal who lays eggs. The rohu has scales but is a fish. The dolphin lives in water but is a mammal.

items.p: Draw a shark, a dolphin and a penguin with the same smooth shape. Under each, write one clue that shows her real group.
items.a: Three similar shapes labelled with gills (shark), lungs and milk (dolphin), and feathers (penguin).
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same shape three times and a different body clue under each that shows her real group.

items.p: Why do fish gills have many thin folds?
opts: More of the gill touches the water, so more oxygen passes in
The folds make the fish heavier
The folds keep the water warm
items.why: Oxygen passes in where a gill touches the water. Many thin folds give a big area in a small space, just as powdered sugar touches water in more places than a lump.

items.p: Out of 16 animal cards, a rule leaves out 2 and lets in 3. How many animals break the rule?
items.why: 2 plus 3 is 5. The rule breaks on 5 animals, whether it leaves them out or lets them in.

items.p: A bat is in the 'can fly' group and in the 'feeds milk' group. Which group is more useful for finding her relatives? Explain.
items.a: The 'feeds milk' group, because milk is a clue that comes from a shared ancestor with mammals such as cats and cows. Flying has appeared in birds, insects and bats separately.
items.why: A strong answer picks the milk group and says that flying appeared several times, while milk follows the family.

items.p: A caterpillar has a backbone.
items.why: False. A caterpillar is the young stage of an insect, and insects have no backbone.

applications: Vets treat reptiles, birds and mammals differently, because the groups differ in how they breathe, keep warm and feed.
Doctors identify snakes as vipers or non-vipers to choose the right treatment for a snakebite.
Conservation workers protect animals such as dugongs, who must surface to breathe, by setting up reserves and freeing animals from nets.
Fisheries managers sort the catch by group, so that dolphins, turtles and sharks caught by accident can be released safely.
Museums arrange skeletons by their matching bones, so visitors can see which animals share a plan.
Drug researchers study animals with no backbone, such as cone snails, whose venom led to a painkiller.
Farmers sort animals as ruminants, birds or fish to plan feed, housing and medicines.
Wildlife researchers use DNA to tell which animals are related, and to find animals not yet named.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animals are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: About 1.5 million kinds of animals have names. One estimate from 2011 suggests there may be about 8.7 million kinds of animals, plants and fungi with cell nuclei, and most are not named yet. Nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Which animal branched off first from the rest: the sponge or the comb jelly?
open_questions.why_open: Studies of DNA give different answers, and scientists still argue about it.

open_questions.q: Why did some fish first crawl onto land?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils show when it happened, about 375 million years ago, but scientists debate why. Ideas include drying pools, food on the shore and escape from big hunters.

open_questions.q: Do animals with no backbone, such as the octopus, have minds like ours?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can see inside another mind. We judge by what an animal does, and octopuses solve problems, use tools and seem to learn.

open_questions.q: What were feathers first for, before birds could fly?
open_questions.why_open: Some small dinosaurs had feathers but could not fly. Scientists debate whether feathers first kept them warm, helped them show off or helped them glide.

open_questions.q: If there is life on other planets, could we sort it into our groups?
open_questions.why_open: We know only one tree of life on Earth. If life elsewhere began separately, our groups might not fit at all. We have no evidence yet either way.

maths.problem: In the Rule Test, rule 1 let in 6 of the 16 animal cards. What fraction of the cards is that? Write it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: 6 out of 16 is the fraction 6 over 16. Divide the top and bottom by 2, and you get 3 over 8.
maths.context: In the Rule Test, you tested the rule 'animals that live in water are fish' on 16 animal cards.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the whole group broke the rule, so you can compare rules even when the number of cards changes.

maths.problem: The bar chart shows how many of the 16 animals broke each rule. How many more animals broke rule 1 than rule 4?
maths.explain: The bar for rule 1 is 6 and the bar for rule 4 is 2. 6 take away 2 is 4.
maths.context: In the Rule Test, the bars show the animals that broke each of the five rules. These are the results you can expect.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which rule broke most, and the gap between two bars tells you how much worse one rule was.

maths.problem: Eight animals are put in two rings: Flies, and Has feathers. The animals are a crow, a bat, a penguin, an ostrich, a cow, a cat, a gecko and a cobra. How many animals are in neither ring?
maths.explain: The crow is in both rings. The bat flies, so she is only in the Flies ring. The penguin and the ostrich have feathers, so they are only in the Has feathers ring. That is 4 animals in a ring. The cow, the cat, the gecko and the cobra are in neither ring, so 8 take away 4 is 4.
maths.why_maths: A Venn diagram shows how two rules overlap, and counting the animals in each part shows where a rule lets in or leaves out animals.

maths.problem: About 19 of every 20 kinds of animal have no backbone. A museum labels 400 kinds of animals in the same proportion. How many of them have a backbone?
maths.explain: 400 divided by 20 is 20 groups of 20. In each group of 20 kinds, 1 has a backbone, so 20 groups give 20 kinds with a backbone.
maths.why_maths: A ratio shows how unequal the two halves of the animals are, and lets you work out the size of one half in a smaller collection.

maths.problem: A Ganges river dolphin comes up to breathe every 2 minutes. How many times does she come up in one hour?
maths.explain: One hour is 60 minutes. 60 divided by 2 is 30.
maths.why_maths: Counting how often an animal must breathe turns the time she can stay under into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: A child can hold her breath for 30 seconds. A sperm whale can stay under for 60 minutes. How many times longer is the whale's time?
maths.explain: 60 minutes is 60 times 60 seconds, which is 3,600 seconds. 3,600 divided by 30 is 120. Always put both times in the same unit first.
maths.context: In the Hold Your Breath test, you timed your own breath hold and compared it with air-breathing animals who live in water.
maths.why_maths: To compare two times you put them in the same unit and divide, and the answer shows how many times longer one is.

maths.problem: In the Lump or Powder test, the whole sugar cube took 240 seconds to dissolve and the powder took 40 seconds. How many times faster was the powder?
maths.explain: 240 divided by 40 is 6. The powder was 6 times faster.
maths.context: In the Lump or Powder test, you dissolved sugar in three forms. These times are made up.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two times shows how much the shape of the sugar changed the speed, which is the same idea as a gill with many folds.

maths.problem: A child breathes out 20 times a minute at rest. How many breaths is that in one hour? Explain how you worked it out.
maths.explain: There are 60 minutes in an hour. 20 times 60 is 1,200.
maths.context: In the Hold Your Breath test, you counted your breaths in one minute.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a count per minute by the minutes in an hour shows how much work the lungs do in a whole hour.

maths.problem: There are about 400,000 kinds of beetle and about 75,000 kinds of animals with a backbone. About how many times as many kinds of beetle are there? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: 400,000 divided by 75,000 is about 5.3, which rounds to 5. Beetles have about five times as many kinds as all the animals with a backbone.
maths.why_maths: Estimating shows how unequal the groups of animals are, without needing the exact numbers.

roots.context: We have tested sorting rules against animals that break them, and followed the backbone family tree. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: A lungfish is a closer relative of a cow than of a salmon. The fish branch that crawled onto land became frogs, lizards, birds, mammals and us. So the word fish names a way of life in water, not one family. By family, we are inside that branch.
deep_truth.habit: We picture the five groups as five separate boxes, and fish as the box farthest from us. But boxes made from looks and ways of life can cut one family in two, and the family tree has no gap between fish and us.
deep_truth.evidence: In the rule test, 'lives in water' put a dolphin with the fish. A lungfish has lungs and fins with bones. Her genes are closer to land animals than to a salmon. And a 375-million-year-old fossil called Tiktaalik had fins with wrist bones.

three.who_am_i: You are a mammal, and by family you are also a branch of the fish that crawled onto land. Your arm has the same bones as a bat's wing and a dolphin's flipper.
three.what_is_life: Every animal with a backbone came from one very old ancestor. Fish, frogs, lizards, crows and cows are all her descendants, so they are cousins.
three.what_is_this_world: Most animals in the world have no backbone, 19 of every 20 kinds. The world is mostly theirs, and we are a small branch of the animals.

roots.thread: More than 500 million years ago, the first small swimmers with a backbone lived in the sea. Their young changed a little in each generation, and the branches split again and again. One branch grew jaws, one grew fleshy fins, and one crawled onto land. Later, eggs with a waterproof skin let animals breed away from water, and then feathers and milk appeared. When we sort by clues that come from ancestors, we are finding where the branches join. All animals with a backbone are one family, and the five groups are five of its branches.

science.text: All animals with a backbone share one ancestor, and the lungfish is the closest living relative of animals who walk on land. Her genome was read in 2021.
Whether birds should still count as their own group, or as a branch of the reptiles, is a question about names, and biologists still argue about it.

other_view.who: Ernst Mayr, a well-known biologist of the 1900s, and others who agreed with him
other_view.view: A good group should reflect how animals live and how much they have changed, as well as who their ancestors were. By this view, birds are different enough from lizards to be a group of their own, and fish are a sensible group, even if the family tree cuts across them.

practice.title: Breathing with the animals
practice.say: Sit still. Put one hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly and feel your lungs fill with air. A dolphin, a crow, a gecko and a cow breathe in the same air with lungs like yours. A frog breathes it through her skin as well. A fish takes the same oxygen from the water with gills. Breathe out slowly three times. Think of one air moving through all of them.
practice.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly. Feel your lungs fill. Dolphins and crows breathe the same air. Breathe out three times.

Every expected count was worked out card by card: rule 1 lets in 6 and leaves out 0, rule 2 lets in 1 and leaves out 2, rule 3 lets in 3 and leaves out 1, rule 4 lets in 2 and leaves out 0, and rule 5 has none. The line 'Young' on the Russell's viper and whale shark cards must not mention milk, or the milk rules break. Hold Your Breath is done sitting down, with a stop whenever the child wants to, and the star jumps are skipped for a child with asthma. how_we_found_out.story: In 1799 a dried skin of a strange animal reached Britain from New South Wales. It had fur, a flat bill like a duck and webbed feet. The scientist George Shaw wondered whether someone had sewn the parts together as a trick. It was real, and it was a platypus. The next puzzle was her eggs. Aboriginal people had long said the platypus lays eggs. Most European scientists did not believe it, because they thought every animal with fur and milk must give birth to live young. So for decades the question stayed open. In 1884 a young Scottish scientist, William Caldwell, hired many Aboriginal people to help him find platypuses and echidnas in Queensland. In late August he found an egg inside an echidna and saw a platypus lay one. He sent a short telegram to a scientific meeting in Montreal. It said that these animals lay eggs. Scientists then changed the rule. A mammal is an animal that feeds milk. Live birth was not needed.
how_we_found_out.who: George Shaw, William Caldwell, and the Aboriginal people who had always known
how_we_found_out.when: 1799 (the first skin described) and 1884 (the eggs shown)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That an animal with fur and milk must give birth to live young, so an animal that lays eggs could not be a mammal. Caldwell found the eggs in 1884, and scientists changed the rule to milk.
how_we_found_out.art: A nineteenth-century scientist in a tent in the Queensland bush holding a platypus egg in his palm while an Aboriginal man points at a stream.
